name: Memory conformity
statement: When two people who saw the same event discuss it, each takes details from the other's account and later reports them as things they saw themselves.
meaning: The claim is about a specific channel for memory error: another person who was there. Classic misinformation studies deliver the false detail through a leading question or a written narrative, and the implied author is an experimenter who presumably knows the answer. A co-witness is different. The source is a peer, present in the room, no better placed than the listener, and the listener has every reason to treat their memory as fallible. Two laboratory traditions test whether the error travels anyway. In the social contagion paradigm a confederate slips items that were never there into a joint recall session. In the co-witness paradigms the two people watch versions of the same film that differ in a handful of details, believe they watched the same thing, discuss it, and are then tested alone. Both ask the same question: does the other person's report change what this person later says they remember. The forensic interest is that real witnesses talk. Where the effect matters is the gap between what a statement claims to be, an independent account, and what it may be, a version of somebody else's.

origin.who: Daniel B. Wright, Gail Self and Chris Justice
origin.note: The name comes from the title of their two experiments on post-event information delivered by another person. That paper could not be obtained, and what it did is described here only from later papers that cite it. Roediger, Meade and Bergman named the same phenomenon the social contagion of memory a year later, working from Asch rather than from eyewitness research, and the two literatures ran in parallel for years. The paper the forensic field is built on is Gabbert, Memon and Allan's dyad procedure of 2003.

evidence: Roediger, Meade and Bergman ran 24 Washington University undergraduates through six household scenes, each shown for 15 or 60 seconds and containing an average of 23.8 objects. A confederate posing as a second participant took turns recalling six items per scene. For three of the six scenes he slipped in two items that had not been there, one that a pilot group had listed as expected in such a scene, a toaster in a kitchen, and one it had not, oven mitts. Tested alone afterwards, with accuracy stressed, participants recalled the suggested items on 22% of occasions against 6% for the same items when they had not been suggested, F(1, 22) = 23.87, p < .01. Expected items travelled better than unexpected ones, 33% against 11%. The shorter viewing time produced the larger effect, 22% against 10%. Most of the false recall was not experienced as recollection. Falsely recalled contagion items drew a know judgement 17% of the time and a remember judgement 5% of the time. Meade and Roediger took the paradigm through four experiments. They warned 37 participants between the joint and the individual test that the other person had made mistakes, and analysed 36 after dropping one who suspected the confederate. The warning cut the contagion effect from .30 to .11, and the effect survived it, t(17) = 2.15. The warning also cost accuracy: correct items the confederate had recalled were later recalled .37 of the time under warning against .47 without it. Suggesting an item four times in written protocols produced a larger effect than suggesting it once, .32 against .09, F(2, 28) = 21.56. Suggesting it once did not beat not suggesting it at all, .15 against .06, t(14) = 1.58. Gabbert, Memon and Allan moved the design to pairs who each watched a different video of the same staged crime and believed they had watched the same one. Their abstract reports that 71% of the witnesses who discussed the event went on to recall at least one of two items they could only have got from the discussion, and that susceptibility did not differ between adults aged 18 to 30 and adults aged 60 to 80. Bodner, Musch and Azad ran that procedure again on 120 Calgary students and got 74% in the discussion group against 10% in a control group. Gabbert, Memon and Wright then taped and transcribed the discussions of 64 of 66 participants shown four pairs of complex pictures differing in two details each. Whoever mentioned a contested item first usually won. First mentioners reported their own version at test 79% of the time; recipients managed 32%, and reported the partner's version instead 35% of the time. Arguing bought nothing here. Disputes followed 39% of mentions and did not predict who was influenced, chi-square(1) = 1.06, p = .30. A second experiment with 58 participants and a staged break-in sorted the details by type. Added details, mentioned by a partner but absent from one's own film, were the most contagious at 45%, ahead of contradicted details at 29% and details one had seen but the partner omitted at 10%. Only the gap between contradicted and omitted reached the .05 level, chi-square(1) = 4.74, p = .03; the gap between added and contradicted did not, chi-square(1) = 2.84, p = .08. The channel matters as well as the content. Gabbert, Memon, Allan and Wright tested 210 people, 108 aged 17 to 33 and 102 aged 58 to 80, on four items of misinformation about a filmed robbery. It arrived either in conversation with a confederate or embedded in a written narrative they were asked to read. Of the four items, the confederate condition produced 1.77 and the narrative condition 1.27, against 0.03 in a control group, F(1, 136) = 5.65, p = .019. The younger group reported more misinformation than the older, 1.82 against 1.21, F(1, 136) = 8.71, p = .004, with no interaction between age and condition. A footnote records that people in the confederate condition also reported more correct information, and that a combined analysis of proportions leaves the interaction between item type and condition non-significant. Witnesses often are not alone. Paterson and Kemp screened 773 Australian psychology undergraduates. Three quarters had witnessed a serious event, most often a physical assault, and 86% of those reported at least one other witness present, a mean of 6.77 and a median of 3. Of the 60 whose follow-up questionnaires were analysed, 86% had discussed the event with a co-witness and 63% had spoken about it immediately.

replication.headline: A ten-country replication of the co-witness procedure found the effect in every sample, with a pooled Hedges' g of 1.70, and located almost all of it in the cases where the listener let the other account stand.
replication.detail: Garry, French, Kinzett and Mori ran the procedure this rests on at Victoria University of Wellington. Forty students sat in pairs wearing polarising glasses and watched what they believed was one film of a tradesman working in a house and stealing from it. Correct answers at test ran at .79 for non-discussed details and .34 for discussed ones, t(39) = 6.82, p < .01, Cohen's d = 1.11. Ito and 18 co-authors repeated it in Brazil, Canada, Colombia, India, Japan, Malaysia, Poland, Portugal, Turkey and the United Kingdom, N = 486, with the second batch of five samples preregistered. Pairs sat side by side wearing filtered glasses, answered questions together in a way that forced the differences into the open, then took a recognition test alone. Recognition accuracy on discussed items fell below accuracy on non-discussed items in all ten samples, all ps < .001, F(1, 405) = 687.57 for the discussion factor with partial eta squared of .63. Pooling the ten new samples gave g = 1.70, 95% CI [1.40, 1.99], Z = 11.17, and adding Garry and colleagues' New Zealand sample gave g = 1.67, 95% CI [1.40, 1.94], Z = 12.19. The authors put the New Zealand estimate at g = 1.46, 95% CI [0.85, 2.07], which is their own recomputation rather than a figure the 2008 paper prints. The size of the effect varied, from a 34-point accuracy gap in Colombia to 64 points in Japan, and the interaction with country was reliable, F(9, 405) = 2.46, p = .010. No pairwise country comparison met the corrected threshold the authors set at .001, the closest being Japan against Canada at p = .012 and Japan against Colombia at p = .016. The moderator that explains the spread is not culture but whether the listener pushed back. Across the ten samples 708 discussed items went undisputed and 58 were disputed. Where the co-witness's answer went unchallenged, the listener later gave that wrong answer in 626 of 708 cases, or 88.4%. Where it had been challenged, one case in 58 went wrong. Disputes were not spread evenly: 30 of the 58 came from the Canadian sample and 10 from the Colombian, four samples recorded none at all, and Japan was one of them. Restricted to undisputed items, accuracy no longer differed across countries, chi-square(9) = 13.92, p = .125. Ito and colleagues point out that this does not fit a collectivism story, because Colombia is the most collectivist of the ten countries on Hofstede's index and Canada among the most individualist. The pattern repeats online and under preregistration. Kękuś, Szpitalak, Polczyk and Barzykowski ran 36 Polish pairs over a video call. Among the 66 of 72 participants who received any misinformation, accuracy was .74 on non-discussed items and .38 on discussed ones, F(1, 65) = 54.06, Hedges' g = 1.17, 95% CI [0.68, 1.69]. Among the 36 who disputed something at least once, accuracy on disputed items was .84 against .17 on undisputed ones, g = 1.84, 95% CI [1.28, 2.47]. A Stage 2 registered report by Kękuś, Chylińska, Szpitalak, Polczyk, Ito, Mori and Barzykowski tested 174 people and analysed 126. Accuracy ran at .53 on non-discussed items against .19 on misdirected ones, F(1, 124) = 85.27, partial eta squared .41. The technique they were testing as a remedy, reinforced self-affirmation, left the effect where it was.

limits: This entry covers discussion between adults who witnessed the same event. It does not cover children's suggestibility or interrogative suggestibility, which the suggestibility entry carries, nor implanted childhood events and the word-list paradigm, which the false memory entry carries, nor collaborative recall as a way of improving accuracy. Two papers could not be read. Gabbert, Memon and Allan (2003) and Wright, Self and Justice (2000) were sought on 21 September 2026 at Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, CORE, the Internet Archive, and the Aberdeen, Abertay, Royal Holloway, Goldsmiths and Sussex repositories, and no full text was found. The publisher pages for both return a bot challenge rather than a paywall notice, so a reader on a different connection may get further. The 71% and the age comparison are quoted from the abstract at Crossref, and Bodner, Musch and Azad's rerun of the same procedure is given alongside them. What the 2000 paper did is taken from the descriptions in Gabbert, Memon, Allan and Wright (2004) and Bodner, Musch and Azad (2009), and no figure from it is printed here. Three papers the previous version of this entry recorded as unobtainable were obtained on the same date. Garry, French, Kinzett and Mori (2008) was read in full from Kazuo Mori's page at researchmap. Gabbert, Memon, Allan and Wright (2004) was read in full from the Abertay repository. Wright, Memon, Skagerberg and Gabbert (2009) was read in full from Goldsmiths Research Online. The Ito figures were read from the author accepted manuscript in the Warwick repository, not the version of record, which was sought at the publisher and at the Rosario, Jagiellonian, Middle East Technical and Minho repositories and not obtained; the last four were unreachable from this connection. The manuscript disagrees with itself. Its results section gives g = 1.67, 95% CI [1.40, 1.94] with the New Zealand sample and g = 1.70, 95% CI [1.40, 1.99] without it. Its discussion pairs the 1.70 with the 1.94 interval. Whether the published version fixes this is still unchecked. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and OpenAlex on 21 September 2026 for a meta-analysis of the memory conformity literature as a whole returned none; the pooled figure quoted here covers eleven runs of one procedure. The paradigms also bound what they show. The details at stake are peripheral, a red cap or a green car, and the co-witness is usually a stranger met minutes earlier in a psychology department. Nothing here establishes how long a conformed detail lasts, whether it survives a formal police interview, or what happens when the disputed fact is who committed the crime.
misreadings: The 71% is treated as the rate at which discussion corrupts memory. It is a headcount, not an item rate: 71% of the witnesses who discussed the event reported at least one of two details they could only have heard from the other person. The number that describes items is Ito and colleagues' 88.4%, and it is conditional. It applies to the 708 cases in which the listener let the other account stand, and where the listener argued the figure was one case in 58. Conformity read as automatic misses the condition attached to it. Kękuś and colleagues put the same point the other way round. Their participants spotted a discrepancy between their own memory and their partner's on 18.4% of misinformed items, and went with the partner on 21.4% of those, against 83.5% of the items where they had noticed nothing. A second reading takes the effect as proof that memory itself has changed. Some of it is people going along with the room. Garry and colleagues found that when a participant accepted a partner's answer during the discussion, they kept it at the private test 85% of the time and reverted to their own answer the other 15%. That 15% is what pure compliance looks like, and it was the smaller share. Roediger and colleagues' remember and know judgements point the same way from the other side. Falsely recalled suggested items drew a know judgement 17% of the time against a remember judgement 5% of the time. The items came back as things the person was confident about rather than things they could picture. The social channel is also read as uniquely potent. Bodner, Musch and Azad compared a discussion group against one that read another live participant's answers, and 74% against 64% is not a gap they could separate from noise, chi-square(1) = 0.89, p = .45. A group that watched both versions of the video beat both. When their participants were then asked where each detail had come from, most attributed the borrowed ones to the partner rather than to the film: 63% of the discussion group reported at least one such detail, and only 14% put it down to the video. Warnings are read as a fix. Meade and Roediger warned participants that the other person had made errors, and the effect fell from .30 to .11 without disappearing. The same warning cut recall of the correct items the confederate had contributed from .47 to .37. Telling a witness to distrust a co-witness costs the accurate information along with the inaccurate. The influence is also read as purely destructive. Roediger and colleagues noted that where their confederate recalled all six items correctly, participants later recalled 43% of those items against 26% for items neither person had mentioned, and flagged the comparison as tentative because it was not counterbalanced. Updating a memory from someone who saw the same thing is usually a good bet, and the false memories are the price. The last misreading is procedural. Memory conformity is not a claim that eyewitnesses are unreliable; it is a claim about what happens to independence when they talk. Paterson and Kemp's respondents talked 86% of the time.
